data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise defining relative clauses with who, which, that, where and whose.
learningPoints: Use who for people and which for things.
Use that for people or things in many defining clauses.
Omit the relative pronoun only when it is the object.
Do not use commas around defining relative clauses.

sections.explain: WHO introduces a defining relative clause about a person.

words.word: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
The woman which lives next door is a doctor.
The woman who she lives next door is a doctor.

sections.explain: WHICH introduces a defining relative clause about a thing.

words.word: The book which is on the table is mine.
The book who is on the table is mine.
The book which it is on the table is mine.

sections.explain: THAT can replace WHICH in many defining relative clauses.

words.word: The phone that I bought is already broken.
The phone that I bought it is already broken.
The phone what I bought is already broken.

sections.explain: WHERE introduces a defining clause about a place.

words.word: This is the café where we first met.
This is the café which we first met there.
This is the café who we first met.

sections.explain: WHOSE shows that something belongs to a person or thing.

words.word: I know a man whose daughter is a pilot.
I know a man who his daughter is a pilot.
I know a man which daughter is a pilot.

sections.explain: When the relative pronoun is the object, it can sometimes be omitted.

words.word: The film we watched was excellent.
The film watched we was excellent.
The film we watched it was excellent.

sections.explain: Do not omit the relative pronoun when it is the subject of the relative clause.

words.word: The man who called you is waiting outside.
The man called you is waiting outside, meaning he was the caller.
The man who he called you is waiting outside.

sections.explain: THAT can often replace WHO in a defining clause.

words.word: The person that helped me was very kind.
The person that he helped me was very kind.
The person which helped me was very kind.

sections.summary: Avoiding commas in a defining clause.
sections.explain: A defining relative clause is essential to identify the noun, so commas are not used.

words.word: Students who arrive late must report to reception.
Students, who arrive late, must report to reception, meaning only late students.
Students who they arrive late must report to reception.

sections.summary: Using a relative clause after a thing.
sections.explain: Use WHICH or THAT when the antecedent is a thing.

words.word: I need a computer that can run this program.
I need a computer who can run this program.
I need a computer that it can run this program.
